articles.title: Raud Ungdom: Raudt vil halvere støtta til ungdomspartiet
articles.content:
Ifølge generalsekretær i Raud Ungdom, Zelda Hasle Borgersrud Øgrim, har sentralstyret i Raudt foreslått å halvere den årlege støtta til ungdomspartiet.

– På landsstyremøtet skal budsjett for 2027 opp, og då har sentralstyret i Raudt vedtatt ei innstilling til landsstyremøtet på at pengestøtta skal kuttest frå to til éin million kroner i 2027, seier ho.

Ho fortel at dette er ein femtedel av det totale budsjettet til RU, og at eit vedtak vil få store konsekvensar.

– Det vil ha mykje å seie for oss, særleg i eit valkampår, seier Øgrim.

NRK har tatt kontakt med Raudt, men dei har foreløpig ikkje kommentert saka.

Rød Ungdom

Rød Ungdom (RU) er ungdomsorganisasjonen til partiet Rødt. Organisasjonen ble grunnlagt i 1963, og hadde tidligere navnet Sosialistisk Ungdomsforbund. I 2024 ble Amrit Kaur valgt til leder i RU.

articles.title: Nordic Mining ber om nytt kortsiktig lån
articles.content:
Nordic Mining seier situasjonen for dotterselskapet «Engebø Rutil og Garnet» er «kritisk» – og ber långivarar om meir pengar.

Det kjem fram i ei børsmelding frå selskapet onsdag kveld.

Selskapet fekk i første omgang utsett krav og rentebetalingar fram til 15. oktober, men den fristen passerte utan at ein permanent avtale var klar.

No ber selskapet obligasjonseigarane om å stemme ja til ein pakke med mellombelse tiltak.

Selskapet ønsker å låne inntil 60 millionar kroner for å dekke rekningar. Dette skal finansierast av ein ny investor og eksisterande långivarar til ei rente på 17,5 prosent.

I tillegg ber selskapet om å få utsette rentebetalingar og unntak frå lånevilkår enn så lenge. Selskapet skriv at dei har fått positive signal frå obligasjonseigarane, men at det ikkje er signert ein avtale enno.

Samstundes jobbar Nordic Mining med industrielle aktørar om ei meir langsiktig løysing, står det i meldinga.

Von der Leyen understreker at den sikkerhetspolitiske og klimamessige utviklingen i nord angår hele Europa direkte.

– Arktis er et sted hvor geopolitikkens tektoniske plater kolliderer. Og det er ikke noen andres yttergrense. Det er en del av Den europeiske union, sier hun.

                        Family immigration appeals in Norway take over 310 days to process, the krone hits its strongest level in over three years, and more news this Tuesday.

Family immigration appeals in Norway take over ten months as processing times increase

In Norway, applicants whose residency or family immigration applications are rejected by the Directorate of Immigration (UDI) have the right to appeal. The case is first reviewed again by UDI; if the agency maintains its rejection, the appeal is forwarded to the Immigration Appeals Board (UNE).

However, according to new figures reported by multicultural newspaper Utrop, families navigating this appeals process at UNE are now waiting an average of 310 days for a ruling.

The statistics, which cover 437 family reunification appeals processed up to September, show that processing times keep increasing, leaving spouses, cohabitants, and children facing months of prolonged legal uncertainty.

Crucially, for those appealing a family immigration refusal, the ten-month wait only covers the appeal phase at UNE. Including UDI’s initial assessment after receiving the application, which now takes about 18 months, the total wait time is over 28 months before getting a final answer.

Regarding the outcome of the appeals, nearly one in five cases (18 percent) ended with UNE overturning or partly reversing UDI’s original rejection.

The board’s data also shows a big difference between case types. Ordinary asylum appeals were processed much faster at 212 days, with only 7 percent of asylum decisions overturned.

This shows that the proportion of overturned decisions was significantly higher in family cases, and that asylum cases were processed 98 days faster than family immigration cases.

READ MORE: Who actually decides immigration and asylum cases in Norway?

Norwegian krone hits its strongest level in over three years

On Monday, the euro fell below 10.56 kroner, its lowest exchange rate against the krone since early 2023, more than three and a half years, according to business news site E24.

The krone has also gained against the US dollar, although it has fluctuated a little more than the euro.

The dollar fell below 9.42 kroner in recent days after hovering near the 10 krone mark at the start of the year.

Financial strategists explained the krone’s rise is due to several market factors: high oil and gas prices, which boost revenues, and Norway’s high policy interest rate, which Norges Bank has maintained while several other central banks have moved to cut.

In short, higher interest rates make Norwegian assets more attractive to investors, and energy export revenues continue to boost the country’s finances.

"We are still in what we can call an ideal regime for the krone. We benefit from good terms of trade, there are high prices for oil and gas, and the underlying risk appetite is good," said Handelsbanken strategist Nils Kristian Knudsen.

Looking ahead, Nordea analysts predict the euro could fall to 10.50 kroner in the next three months and possibly reach 10.25 kroner by the summer of 2027. "If the prediction is correct, a trip to the south next summer could become cheaper for us Norwegians," E24 explained.

Norwegian households used a record 6.8 terawatt-hours (TWh) of electricity during the third quarter of 2026 (July to September), a 7.9 percent increase from the same period last year, according to  data from Statistics Norway (SSB).

This is the highest third-quarter figure since SSB started tracking in 2020.

The increase was mostly due to higher home heating demand after unusually cool weather in August and September (months that are typically among the mildest in the country).

At the same time, overall electricity production fell by 8.6 percent due to low water reservoirs and weaker hydropower generation in southern and western regions.

"There was a decline in hydroelectric power production in all price areas, except in Northern Norway, where production increased by around 16 percent from the third quarter of last year," said Magne Holstad, senior adviser at Statistics Norway.

​Norwegian vocabulary: strømforbruket - the electricity consumption

Norway faces pressure to add tariffs on Chinese EVs as imports rise

Norway could be forced to introduce EU tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles in exchange for remaining part of a new European industrial initiative.

On Friday, France and Germany agreed on a joint proposal to strengthen the European automotive industry against competition from countries like China.

According to the draft seen by the newspaper Aftenposten, non-EU countries like Norway and the UK could only join the proposed 'Made in Europe' initiative if they follow the EU’s trade protection rules.

The European Union recently set duties of up to 45 percent on Chinese-made electric cars, but Norway has not imposed similar charges.

The Norwegian government now faces a difficult legal and economic choice.

As the country is part of the single market through the EEA agreement but is not in the EU customs union, it cannot legally impose retaliatory tariffs under World Trade Organization (WTO) rules, since those tariffs must protect domestic manufacturing, and Norway does not make its own cars.

However, if Norway cannot join the 'Made in Europe' framework, Norwegian companies could lose access to European public contracts and industrial subsidies.

This political pressure comes as Chinese goods have flooded the Norwegian market. The Road Traffic Information Council said that chinese car brands made up 13.7 percent of new car sales in 2025, and that among private buyers, the share has risen to 19.4 percent so far in 2026.

Nine out of ten electric buses imported to Norway are also Chinese

Overall, imports from China rose by 18 percent, according to a survey by Energi og Klima.

articles.content:

Politiet vil ikkje gå nærare inn på operative tiltak eller detaljar rundt besøket, men seier besøket vil kunne få konsekvenser for trafikken i Oslo.

– I periodar vil det kunne føre til einskilde trafikale utfordringar i sentrum.

articles.content:
Ti brukerstyrte personlige assistenter går ut i streik fra tirsdag klokken 10, opplyser Fagforbundet i en pressemelding.

Det skjer etter at meklingen mellom Fagforbundet og NHO Geneo ikke førte frem.

Medlemmene som blir tatt ut i streik jobber ved Human Care i Ullensaker, Horten, Sande, Høvik, Bærum, Kleppe, Drammen, Kongsberg og Tverlandet.

Uenigheten handler om lønnstillegg for ubekvem arbeidstid.

– Vi måtte gå til streik for to år siden for å oppnå bransjestandard i lønn. Nå må vi dessverre gjøre det igjen. Det er provoserende, sier nestleder i Fagforbundet, Line Tollefsen.

Sigurd Løkholm, forhandlingsleder for NHO Geneo, sier de har strukket seg langt for å finne en løsning.

– Det er beklagelig at Fagforbundet velger å ta ut BPA-virksomheter i streik. Dette rammer vedtakseiere og pårørende som er avhengige av tjenestene de tilbyr, uttaler Løkholm i en pressemelding.

articles.content:
Ismail A. Hussein trekker seg fra Oslo Venstre sin bystyregruppe og melder seg ut av partiet. Det skriver han i et facebook-innlegg mandag ettermiddag.

                        Those living in Oslo have long perceived the city's distinct residential divisions, and new academic research now provides data to back up those impressions.

A study by researchers at NOVA at Oslo Metropolitan University, published by forskning.no, investigated how families in the capital region choose where to live, revealing clear patterns.

Using data from over 20,000 family moves between 1993 and 2017, the study showed that despite city policies to encourage integration, families’ choices still lead to demographic divisions in Oslo.

​Specifically, Norwegian-born parents from all income and wealth levels avoid moving to neighbourhoods with high proportions of non-Western immigrants.

​Lead researcher Professor Lena Magnusson Turner said this trend is worrying. “Although policy facilitates people from different socio-economic classes living in the same neighbourhood, we see that the population chooses differently.”

​Turner explained that people also look for neighbours who are similar to themselves, while less affluent families actively avoid areas where they would feel financially inferior.

“When people move and have the opportunity to choose, they move to neighbourhoods where they find people who are like them. People don't seek out neighbourhoods where the inequalities are too great,” she said.

​The study also established that accumulated wealth influences neighbourhood selection far more than income, leading the most affluent households to cluster in specific areas.

​When looking at families with children, the study revealed that parents with daughters care more about the economic status of their neighbours than parents with sons. “We think it's about ideas parents have about protecting their girls to a greater extent, while assuming boys can handle themselves,” Turner added.

                        Norwegian police said Wednesday that they had arrested five people as part of an investigation into aggravated fraud against a NATO agency.

The people, who were arrested in the region of Bergen in western Norway, are suspected of "over-invoicing" the NATO Support and Procurement Agency (NSPA) for services provided to NATO ships in Norwegian ports between 2021 and 2025.

The overcharges are more than one million euros ($1.12 million), police said in a statement.

"Defence sector budgets are increasing worldwide, which entails an increased risk of economic crime. This is an area we are monitoring closely," said Marianne Bender, Senior Public Prosecutor at Norway's national economic crime unit.

"If NATO has been defrauded, there will be a tough crackdown," she added.

Romanian and German police have also carried out searches at several companies in Romania and Germany suspected of being linked to the same case, according to the statement.

articles.content:

                        Navigating Norway's immigration laws can be complex. Fortunately, several organisations provide free guidance to people facing immigration challenges.

As is the case in most European countries, immigrants and asylum seekers in Norway are fortunate to have access to a number of organisations dedicated to providing free guidance, support, and legal aid.

Whether you're seeking assistance with asylum claims, family immigration cases, permanent residence permits, or citizenship applications, here's where to look if you need free expert advice and support.

READ MORE: Do you need a lawyer in Norway for work permit or residency problems?

NOAS usually supports people navigating the asylum process in Norway. They specialise in asylum cases and offer legal aid to those whose asylum claims have been rejected by the Norwegian Directorate of Immigration (UDI) or the Immigration Appeals Board (UNE).

Furthermore, NOAS extends its services to family immigration cases, permanent residence permits, and citizenship matters.

You can contact them via phone at +47 22 36 56 60 or through their email at post@noas.org

Additionally, if you want to book face-to-face assistance, you can visit NOAS's office at Torggata 22, Oslo, during office hours.

Operated by dedicated students in Oslo, Jussbuss is a great resource for people seeking free legal aid, including assistance with immigration-related matters.

Jussbuss accepts new cases and offers guidance on various legal issues through phone consultations (+47 22 84 29 00) or in-person visits during their office hours at Skippergata 23 in Oslo.

They specialise in immigration, labour, debt issues, social security, tenancy, and prison law.

Launched with the objective of empowering immigrants and refugees, SEIF operates as a voluntary organisation committed to providing support and guidance.

With offices across Norway, SEIF offers a number of services, ranging from information dissemination to assistance with complex immigration matters.

Their areas of assistance include issues with the Norwegian Labour and Welfare Administration (NAV), school, work, residence permits, family reunification, financial problems, forced marriage and honour-related violence, coercion, and more.

They have an open-door policy and commitment to confidentiality.

You can find all the contact information for their offices in Oslo, Kristiansand, Ålesund, Trondheim, Bergen, Stavanger, and Tromsø here.

Catering specifically to women, JURK provides free legal assistance on a number of issues, including immigration matters, thereby addressing the often unique needs of female immigrants and asylum seekers. Along with free legal aid, JURK examines women's need for legal assistance, works to improve the legal position of women, and provides practical legal training for law students.

Staffed by students from the University of Bergen Faculty of Law, Jussformidlingen extends its services to people across Norway, leveraging its expertise to offer guidance and assistance on a wide scope of legal issues on civil law, including immigration challenges. It aims to provide free legal aid, meet the public demand for legal assistance, and offer law students practical experience opportunities.

Serving as the umbrella organisation for various student legal aid entities, Gratis Rettshjelp coordinates efforts to provide assistance on various matters, including immigration. It receives approximately 20,000 inquiries annually.

Offering free legal counsel in multiple cities throughout Norway, Advokatvakten allows people to consult with private lawyers who are members of the Norwegian Bar Association for up to 30 minutes free of charge.

Exclusive to Oslo residents, this municipal service offers free legal advice from private lawyers funded by the Norwegian government. Appointments can be scheduled via phone, online, or through drop-in hours at their office in Storgata 19, Oslo.

Caritas, an independent humanitarian foundation, operates multiple info centres across Norway, including Oslo, Bergen, Trondheim, Stavanger, and Drammen. Several times a week, they offer free legal assistance with specialised lawyers who speak multiple languages.

The organisation has extensive experience handling immigration cases, workplace disputes, and tenancy or landlord issues.

This service is run by licensed Norwegian lawyers through the NGO Flerkulturell.org and offers first-line legal advice in your native language. They have dedicated pages for Spanish, Polish, Ukrainian, Arabic, Lithuanian, and Somali, but can help speakers of any language if you ask.

Their services include help with immigration, child protection, workplace exploitation, and others.

You can contact them through their website, by phone at +47 90 08 51 88, or by email at advokat@klovfjell.no

Catering to residents of northern Norway, this organisation provides legal help facilitated by law students from the University of Tromsø. You can seek their assistance by calling or submitting cases online.

Beyond immigration, there are several other free support services available throughout Norway.

For individuals facing domestic abuse, sexual violence, or threats from a partner or family member, local crisis shelters (krisesentre) like Oslo Krisesenter offer free and confidential protection, emergency accommodation, and legal advice.

Pro-Sentret also supports people who have experienced physical or sexual violence.

For people struggling with severe financial hardship, the Norwegian Labour and Welfare Administration (NAV) offers free debt and financial counseling  as part of its services.

Anyone under 25 can get free legal advice from Young Legal Aid (Ung Rettshjelp), a service designed to help young adults understand their legal rights.

articles.title: Israelske bosettere angrep diplomater på Vestbredden
articles.content:
Israelske bosettere angrep lørdag diplomater på den okkuperte Vestbredden, melder blant annet nyhetsbyrået AFP.

En av de som ble angrepet var en fransk ordfører, Bernard Baudoux.

– Angrepet viser Israels toleranse for bosettervold, sier han til nyhetsbyrået.

Også belgiske og polske diplomater var med i gruppen som ble angrepet.

Belgiske myndigheter har fordømt angrepet. Det har også Israels utenriksminister Gideon Sa’ar, som kaller det et angrep fra opprørere.

Han legger også noe av skylden på diplomatene for å ikke ha «koordinert» med det israelske militæret.

Angrepet skjedde ved landsbyen Taybah, ikke langt fra stedet der flere palestinere og en amerikansk fotograf ble angrepet av bosettere fredag.

Vestbredden

Israelske myndigheter kontrollerer Vestbredden som har vært okkupert av Israel siden 1967, i strid med Folkeretten. Enkelte områder har begrenset palestinsk selvstyre. Store områder på Vestbredden er dominert av nye israelske bosettinger.

Palestina

Palestina er en delvis anerkjent stat i Midtøsten, bestående av Vestbredden og Gazastripen. Området har blitt herjet av krig med blant annet Israel i lang tid. Norge har anerkjent Palestina som en selvstendig stat siden mai 2024.

Israels bosettinger på Vestbredden

Israelske myndigheter bygger stadig flere boliger på okkupert grunn i Øst-Jerusalem og på Vestbredden. Slik bygging er ifølge FN i strid med folkeretten. 600.000 jøder bor i de omlag 140 bosettingene som er bygget siden 1967.
